articles.title: Colorado’s largest wildlife overpass cut I-25 collisions by 91 percent
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Nine months in, North America’s largest wildlife overpass has cut vehicle collisions on a stretch of Interstate 25 in Colorado by 91 percent. Before it opened, that corridor was averaging roughly one deer hit per day during peak migration. The crossing, a 209-by-200-foot structure near the Greenland exit between […]
The post Colorado’s largest wildlife overpass cut I-25 collisions by 91 percent first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Nine months in, North America’s largest wildlife overpass has cut vehicle collisions on a stretch of Interstate 25 in Colorado by 91 percent. Before it opened, that corridor was averaging roughly one deer hit per day during peak migration.

The crossing, a 209-by-200-foot structure near the Greenland exit between Larkspur and Monument, opened in December. It came in ahead of schedule and under budget. Five underpasses and miles of fencing channel animals toward the safe crossings.

One deer a day, then nothing

For decades, I-25 in Douglas and El Paso counties cut across seasonal migration corridors for elk and pronghorn with no way across. Colorado Parks and Wildlife biologist Brandon Marette called it “an effective wall that they had to play Frogger and try to get across.” Pronghorn ranging between Trinidad and Greenland had nowhere to go. The highway averaged roughly one deer hit per day during spring and fall migration.

Elk herds and returning pronghorn

Cameras at the crossing have since recorded elk herds crossing in groups and pronghorn on the west side of I-25 for the first time in decades. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25,” said Chuck Attardo, CDOT Environmental Manager. “And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”

Bears, deer, and coyotes have also been recorded. One image caught an elk cow leading her calf under the highway. Marette said it was the payoff for six years of work.

Not just the big animals

Elk and pronghorn were the primary targets, but wildlife managers didn’t stop there.

Covered pathways for small mammals

Biologists piled wood into corridors on the overpass to give small mammals covered routes across. “So that coyotes, foxes, and hawks don’t pick them off when they’re trying to cross I-25 on the overpass,” Marette said. The Preble’s meadow jumping mouse, which is federally threatened, lives in the area and now uses the crossing. Northern leopard frogs, reptiles, and amphibians are crossing too. “We’re not just focused on the big game species, but also on the smaller,” Marette said.

Native vegetation on the overpass surface is still being established. This year’s drought slowed germination; new topsoil and reseeding are planned for next year.

The economics for Colorado’s wildlife crossings

Under budget, ahead of schedule

The project received $22 million in federal infrastructure funds and $8 million from the state. Contractor Kraemer North America finished it for $15 million, about half the total. Attardo says crossings like this typically recoup their cost in about 15 years through the accidents, property damage, and service costs they prevent. “They pay for themselves in about 15 years because of all those accidents that they prevent. So why wouldn’t you do more of these?”

Funding the next round of crossings

A recently passed state law is expected to generate around $3 million per year for wildlife mitigation projects. That money would go toward matching larger federal grants. CDOT has a list of priority corridors: Raton Pass near the New Mexico border, US-40 near Empire, State Highway 160 near Mesa Verde, East Vail Pass, US-40 near Craig, US-287 near Fort Collins, and several sites near Boulder.

What it takes to make one happen

The Greenland crossing took six years and a coalition: the Federal Highway Administration, CDOT, Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Douglas County, the Douglas Land Conservancy, and the Colorado Cattlemen’s Agricultural Land Trust. Conservation easements on both sides of the highway made it viable.

“Everybody marching in the same direction,” Attardo said. “I really can’t stress enough how important it is to have leadership on your side when you’re trying to do big projects like this.”

The Douglas Land Conservancy holds over 28,500 acres in the region. Executive director Laura Sanford put it simply: “It’s not just for you; it is for everyone.”

articles.personality_title: Colorado’s largest wildlife overpass cuts animal-vehicle collisions by 91%
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Interstate 25 (I-25) in Colorado has long been a dangerous barrier for migrating wildlife like deer, elk, and pronghorn. Every day during migration seasons, many animals were hit by vehicles, causing harm to both animals and drivers.

**What happened**
In December, Colorado opened North America’s largest wildlife overpass near the Greenland exit on I-25. This large bridge, about 209 by 200 feet, allows animals to safely cross over the highway. The project included five underpasses and miles of fencing to guide animals toward these crossings. It took six years to complete and involved many groups working together.

**Impact**
Since the overpass opened, collisions between vehicles and wildlife on this stretch of I-25 have dropped by 91 percent. Cameras have recorded elk and pronghorn using the crossing, some for the first time in decades. Smaller animals like mice, frogs, and coyotes also use the safe paths. The project was finished ahead of schedule and cost less than expected, saving lives and reducing accidents.

Colorado plans to build more wildlife crossings using new state funds combined with federal grants. Several other highways have been identified for future projects to help animals cross safely and reduce accidents. The success of this overpass shows how teamwork and planning can protect wildlife and drivers.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Colorado’s new wildlife overpass has dramatically lowered highway collisions by providing a safe path for animals to cross busy roads.

articles.title: Offshore wind plant to bring jobs boost to Montrose
articles.summary: The new facility will manufacture parts for offshore wind farms in Scottish waters and for overseas markets.
articles.content:
An offshore wind turbine facility is to be created at the Port of Montrose, supporting about 80 jobs.

The factory, which will make components for off-shore wind turbines, is to be run by engineering firm Subsea Micropiles following a £5m investment.

A further £6.7m is being provided by the state-owned Scottish National Investment Bank, with Scottish Enterprise also pledging £1.45m.

First Minister John Swinney, during a visit to the site in Angus, said it would help ensure "benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland".

He also welcomed an announcement from SSE that the Port of Montrose is its preferred location for an operations base for the Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm, which is expected to create a further 100 jobs.

The Berwick project, set to be one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, will see up to 307 turbines generating enough electricity to power up to six million homes.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the creation of a new offshore wind turbine manufacturing facility in Scotland, supported by significant investment and government backing. This development will generate around 80 jobs and supports a major offshore wind farm project expected to power millions of homes, contributing to renewable energy expansion and economic growth. The story has broad significance for climate action, job creation, and energy transition in Scotland and beyond.

It will create about 80 jobs. The project received £5 million from private investment, £6.7 million from the Scottish National Investment Bank, and £1.45 million from Scottish Enterprise.

**Impact** – This factory will help Scotland produce key parts for wind farms locally instead of importing them. articles.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
articles.summary: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.
articles.content:
Sea turtles are known for extraordinary journeys across the ocean. They can navigate using cues from Earth's magnetic field, the sun, and ocean currents, traveling long distances to find food before eventually returning toward the places where they were born to reproduce.

That reputation made one population in the Galápagos especially surprising. Rather than roaming across vast stretches of ocean, these turtles appeared to spend much of their time close to home.

"Here we show that 'yellow-morph' green sea turtles - one of two genetically distinct forms - occupy individual foraging areas which span one or more islands in the Galápagos. We expected them to migrate to distant beaches in the western Pacific to reproduce, yet interestingly, none of our satellite-tagged turtles even left the Galápagos Marine Reserve over the three years of our study," said Dr. John W Rowe, a professor at Alma College in the United States and the corresponding author of a new study in Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science.

Two Distinct Types of Green Sea Turtle

Green sea turtles stand apart from the other six living sea turtle species because adults are primarily vegetarian. Young turtles begin life eating both plants and animals, but as they mature, their diet shifts mainly to seagrasses and algae.

Scientists recognize two genetically distinct forms involved in this study. Yellow morph green sea turtles are generally found across tropical and subtropical parts of the western Pacific, while black morphs occur in the eastern Pacific west of the Americas and south of southern California.

The Galápagos is the only known place where both forms share the same waters. There, yellow and black morphs mingle and feed on the same types of marine vegetation.

They are not completely alike, however. Young yellow morphs tend to grow more quickly than young black morphs, suggesting that there may be physiological differences between them that scientists have not yet fully characterized.

Tracking Turtles Across the Galápagos

Rowe and his colleagues wanted to better understand where yellow morphs spend their time, how much territory they use, and whether they travel between islands within the 198,000 sq km Galápagos Marine Reserve.

In 2015, the team carefully captured nine adults in shallow water near four islands. The group included seven males and two females. Researchers gave the turtles nicknames and attached electronic transmitters that sent location signals to the low orbit Argos satellite network.

The turtles were followed for as long as 418 days. Tracking generally ended when a tag detached or stopped sending signals.

The results revealed a strong preference for shallow coastal habitat. Although the turtles occasionally traveled as far as 25km from shore, most remained much closer to the islands.

Five of the nine spent most of the study near a single island. Bernardo and Sara moved between Isabela and San Cristóbal, while Leandro traveled between Isabela and Española.

Ainoa was the most adventurous of the group. After being tagged near San Cristóbal, she later traveled to Santa Cruz and then to Isabela.

The researchers also noticed a seasonal pattern. Movement between islands occurred only during the cooler period from April through October.

On average, each turtle used a home range covering 1,498 sq km, although the size of that territory differed considerably from one animal to another.

Surprisingly Reluctant To Leave

Taken together, the tracking data suggest that yellow morph green sea turtles living around the Galápagos can be remarkably homebound.

The researchers cautioned that their observations capture only a limited period in the turtles' lives. Longer migrations could occur at other times and therefore may not have appeared during the study.

That possibility is especially important for females.

"Since female yellow-morph green sea turtles are not known to lay eggs on the beaches of the Galápagos, we believe that they will eventually leave the area to return to their natal beaches in the western Pacific. In contrast, some female black-morph green turtles do nest in the Galápagos: depending on the individual, those may be year-round residents in the archipelago, travel to other nearby oceanic islands, or even to feeding grounds off Central and South America," said coauthor Dr. Juan Pablo Muñoz Pérez, a professor at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito in Ecuador.

Protecting a Network of Turtle Habitat

The findings also carry implications for conservation. Because some turtles move among several islands, protecting only one favored feeding location may not be enough.

Researchers emphasized the importance of preserving the coastal waters and routes between islands that the turtles depend on as they move throughout the archipelago.

"Since individual turtles may rely on waters around multiple islands, the quality of habitat that is available for foraging should be maintained intact across all islands, and not allowed to degrade anywhere," said Rowe.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about the behavior of yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos, revealing their strong site fidelity and the importance of coastal habitats within a large marine reserve. This insight has broad conservation implications for protecting multiple island habitats, which benefits biodiversity and ecosystem health in a globally important natural area.
articles.personality_title: Galápagos yellow-morph sea turtles stay close to home, surprising scientists
articles.personality_presentation:

Instead of making long journeys, the turtles stayed within the Galápagos Marine Reserve, moving mostly between nearby islands and coastal areas. Nine turtles were followed for up to 418 days, and none left the protected waters.

**Impact** – This finding is unusual because it shows these turtles depend heavily on local coastal habitats rather than distant migration. It means the Galápagos’ coastal areas are especially important for their survival. The study also highlights that protecting just one island is not enough since turtles use several islands as home.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope to continue studying these turtles for longer periods to see if females eventually travel elsewhere to lay eggs, as no yellow-morph females have been found nesting in the Galápagos. Conservation efforts will need to focus on keeping the coastal habitats across multiple islands healthy to support these turtles.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos live mostly close to home, showing that protecting many island habitats is key to their survival.

articles.title: France puts out massive fire that torched 42,000 hectares and smouldered for 69 days
articles.summary: France's largest wildfire since 1949 has been declared extinguished more than two months after it broke out in southwestern Gironde, forcing the evacuation of around 224,000 people and covering the city of Bordeaux with a thick plume of smoke. The blaze was put under control on August 1, but continued to smoulder underground for weeks.
articles.content:
A wildfire that scorched 42,000 hectares in southwest France has finally been declared extinguished, more than two months after the country's largest blaze since 1949 broke out, authorities said Monday.

The fire erupted in July near the village of Saumos in the Gironde region and forced the evacuation of around 224,000 people as it threatened both the tourist peninsula of Cap-Ferret and the outskirts of Bordeaux.

"The Saumos forest fire, which burned 42,000 hectares this summer, including 37,296 hectares destroyed, is now extinguished," state services wrote in a statement, adding no deaths had been reported.

Read moreFrench wildfires: FRANCE 24 goes on the ground with firefighters

The blaze was put under control on August 1, but continued to smoulder underground for weeks before finally being declared out.

More than 3,300 firefighters took part in the operation, which officials described as the largest firefighting effort in modern French civil security history.

The blaze was the largest recorded in France since a 1949 wildfire in the same region that burned about 50,000 hectares.

France has seen around 98,000 hectares destroyed by wildfires this year, the highest level since 1976, according to provisional figures.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful extinguishing of France's largest wildfire since 1949, which had a significant environmental and social impact. The containment of such a massive fire involving a large-scale firefighting effort and no reported deaths is a meaningful positive development in terms of disaster management and environmental protection.
articles.personality_title: France extinguishes largest wildfire since 1949 after 69 days
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In July 2023, a huge wildfire started near Saumos in southwestern France’s Gironde region. It became the largest wildfire in the country since 1949, burning a massive area and forcing many people to leave their homes.

**What happened** – The fire scorched 42,000 hectares, including 37,296 hectares completely destroyed. Over 224,000 people were evacuated as the fire threatened the tourist area of Cap-Ferret and the city of Bordeaux. More than 3,300 firefighters worked for weeks to control and finally put out the fire. Although the flames stopped on August 1, the fire continued to smoulder underground until it was fully extinguished in late August.

**Impact** – This wildfire was the largest in France in over 70 years and caused a lot of damage to forests and communities. Despite the size and danger, no deaths were reported, showing how well emergency teams managed the crisis. The effort involved thousands of firefighters and was the biggest firefighting operation in modern French history.

**What's next step** – Officials will continue to monitor the area to prevent new fires and support recovery efforts for the damaged forests and towns. Lessons learned from this event will help improve future wildfire responses as climate change increases fire risks.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 69 days and a historic effort by thousands of firefighters, France successfully extinguished its largest wildfire since 1949 without any loss of life.
articles.personality_title_fr: La France éteint le plus grand incendie depuis 1949 après 69 jours
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En juillet 2023, un immense incendie a commencé près de Saumos, dans la région de Gironde, dans le sud-ouest de la France. Il est devenu le plus grand incendie du pays depuis 1949, brûlant une vaste zone et forçant de nombreuses personnes à évacuer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le feu a brûlé 42 000 hectares, dont 37 296 hectares complètement détruits. Plus de 224 000 personnes ont été évacuées alors que le feu menaçait la zone touristique du Cap-Ferret et la ville de Bordeaux. Plus de 3 300 pompiers ont travaillé pendant des semaines pour contrôler et enfin éteindre le feu. Bien que les flammes se soient arrêtées le 1er août, le feu a continué de couver sous terre jusqu’à son extinction complète fin août.

**Impact** – Cet incendie était le plus grand en France depuis plus de 70 ans et a causé beaucoup de dégâts aux forêts et aux communautés. Malgré l’ampleur et le danger, aucune victime n’a été signalée, montrant la bonne gestion de la crise par les équipes d’urgence. L’opération a mobilisé des milliers de pompiers et fut la plus grande de l’histoire moderne de la sécurité civile française.

**Prochaine étape** – Les autorités continueront de surveiller la zone pour prévenir de nouveaux incendies et aider à la reconstruction des forêts et des villes touchées. Les leçons tirées de cet événement permettront d’améliorer la réponse aux incendies futurs, alors que le changement climatique augmente les risques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après 69 jours et un effort historique de milliers de pompiers, la France a réussi à éteindre son plus grand incendie depuis 1949 sans perte humaine.
articles.personality_title_es: Francia apaga el mayor incendio desde 1949 tras 69 días
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En julio de 2023, un gran incendio comenzó cerca de Saumos, en la región de Gironda, en el suroeste de Francia. Se convirtió en el mayor incendio del país desde 1949, quemando una gran área y obligando a mucha gente a evacuar.

**Qué pasó** – El fuego quemó 42,000 hectáreas, incluyendo 37,296 hectáreas completamente destruidas. Más de 224,000 personas fueron evacuadas mientras el incendio amenazaba la zona turística de Cap-Ferret y la ciudad de Burdeos. Más de 3,300 bomberos trabajaron durante semanas para controlar y finalmente apagar el incendio. Aunque las llamas se detuvieron el 1 de agosto, el fuego siguió ardiendo bajo tierra hasta ser completamente extinguido a finales de agosto.

**Impacto** – Este incendio fue el más grande en Francia en más de 70 años y causó muchos daños a los bosques y comunidades. A pesar del tamaño y el peligro, no hubo muertes, lo que muestra la buena gestión de la crisis por parte de los equipos de emergencia. La operación involucró a miles de bomberos y fue la más grande en la historia moderna de la seguridad civil francesa.

**Próximo paso** – Las autoridades seguirán vigilando la zona para evitar nuevos incendios y ayudar en la recuperación de los bosques y pueblos dañados. Las lecciones aprendidas ayudarán a mejorar la respuesta a futuros incendios, ya que el cambio climático aumenta los riesgos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Tras 69 días y un esfuerzo histórico de miles de bomberos, Francia logró apagar su mayor incendio desde 1949 sin perder vidas humanas.
